rule_en: English questions follow the pattern QUASI: Question word, Auxiliary, Subject, Infinitive. Use do/does for the present simple and did for the past simple. With the verb be, invert the subject and the verb and don't add an auxiliary.
examples_en: What kind of books do you read?
Where did you learn English?
How often does your cousin visit you?
Are your parents from the same town?
tip: Never add do/does/did to questions with be: 'Where are you from?', not 'Where do you are from?'

rule_en: Use the present simple for habits, routines, opinions and permanent situations. Remember -s for he/she/it and don't/doesn't in negatives. Frequency adverbs (always, usually, often) go before the main verb.
examples_en: She usually gets on well with new people.
My best friend never worries about small things.
He doesn't look like his father at all.
What do you do at weekends?
tip: 'What does he do?' asks about a job; 'What is he doing?' asks about now.

rule_en: Use the present continuous (be + verb-ing) for things happening now, around now, or temporary situations. Also use it to describe photos and scenes. State verbs (know, want, like, need, believe) are not normally continuous.
examples_en: I'm looking for a black jacket in a medium size.
In this photo, my friends are standing outside the theatre.
She's staying with her aunt until the flat is ready.
Why are you wearing a coat? It's warm today!
tip: For photos use the continuous: 'In this picture, people are dancing.'

topic: past simple: regular and irregular verbs
rule_en: Use the past simple for finished actions in the past, often with a time expression (last year, in 2020, two days ago). Regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs must be learned (go–went, buy–bought, lose–lost). Questions and negatives use did/didn't + base form.
structure: verb-ed / irregular form; did(n't) + base verb
examples_en: We booked the hotel online and paid by card.
I lost my passport on the last day of the holiday.
They didn't enjoy the tour because it rained all day.
Did you take many photos in Istanbul?
tip: Time expressions for the past: yesterday, last week, ago, in 2015, when I was a child.

rule_en: Use the past continuous (was/were + verb-ing) for an action in progress at a moment in the past, often interrupted by a past simple action: I was walking home when it started to rain. Also use it to set the scene in a story.
examples_en: At nine o'clock we were still having breakfast.
She was taking a photo when a bird landed on her head.
The sun was shining and people were sitting in cafes.
What were you doing at midnight?
tip: Long background action → past continuous; short interrupting action → past simple.

rule_en: Time sequencers order events in a story: first, then, after that, later, when, suddenly, finally. Connectors join ideas: because (reason), so (result), but (contrast), although (surprising contrast).
examples_en: First we parked the car, and then we walked to the centre.
Suddenly the dog started to bark.
I was tired, so I went to bed early.
Although it was cold, we sat outside.
tip: because = reason, so = result: 'I stayed home because I was ill' / 'I was ill, so I stayed home.'

rule_en: Use be going to + verb for plans and intentions decided before speaking, and for predictions based on present evidence. Negative: be + not + going to. Questions: be + subject + going to.
examples_en: We're going to rent a car at the airport.
I'm not going to check in any luggage — only hand luggage.
Look at the queue! We're going to wait for hours.
What are you going to do after the flight?
tip: Plan made earlier → going to; instant decision → will.

rule_en: Use the present continuous for fixed future arrangements — plans with a time and place, often written in a diary: We're meeting at six. I'm flying to Moscow on Friday. It is very common with verbs of movement (go, come, leave, arrive).
examples_en: I'm seeing the dentist tomorrow morning.
They're getting married in September.
We're leaving at seven, so don't be late.
She's arriving in Dushanbe on Sunday evening.
tip: Arrangement with a fixed time/place → present continuous; general intention → going to.

rule_en: Defining relative clauses say which person or thing we mean. Use who for people, which for things, that for both, and where for places: A chef is a person who cooks in a restaurant. Don't add a second subject pronoun: 'the man who lives here', not 'the man who he lives here'.
examples_en: A dictionary is a book which explains words.
She's the doctor who helped my grandmother.
That's the cafe where we first met.
I like people that say what they think.
tip: Paraphrasing: if you forget a word, describe it — 'It's a thing which you use for...'

rule_en: Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) with just (a very recent action), already (sooner than expected) and yet (in negatives and questions, until now): I've just finished. She's already done it. Have you washed up yet?
structure: have/has (+ just/already) + participle; ... yet (end of negatives/questions)
examples_en: I've just made the beds.
He's already done the shopping.
Have you cleaned the kitchen yet?
We haven't taken the rubbish out yet.
tip: just/already go in the middle; yet goes at the end.

rule_en: Use the present perfect for recent actions and experiences without a specific time. Use the past simple when the time is stated or finished: I've bought a new bag (recent, no time) vs I bought it last Saturday (time given). Conversations often start in the perfect and continue in the past.
structure: perfect: no time; past simple: finished time
examples_en: I've bought a new jacket. — Really? Where did you buy it?
She's spent all her money. She spent most of it on shoes.
Have you ever returned anything to a shop? — Yes, I returned a shirt last month.
We've been to that shopping centre twice.
tip: Start the topic with the perfect, give the details in the past simple.

rule_en: Compounds with some- appear in positive sentences (something, someone, somewhere); any- in negatives and questions (anything, anyone, anywhere); no- makes the sentence negative with a positive verb (nothing, no one, nowhere). Everything/everyone take a singular verb.
examples_en: I bought something special for the weekend.
Did anyone call while I was out?
There's nothing interesting on TV tonight.
Everyone was excited about the trip.
tip: Don't use two negatives: 'I didn't see anything', not 'I didn't see nothing'.

rule_en: Compare with adjective-er / more + adjective + than. Adverbs usually use more: more quickly. Use as...as for equality and not as...as for difference: He's as tall as his father. It's not as cold as yesterday. Irregular: better, worse, further.
examples_en: The metro is faster than the bus.
She speaks English more fluently than me.
Today isn't as hot as yesterday.
My results are worse than last year.
tip: as...as = the same; not as...as = less.

rule_en: Superlatives compare one thing with the whole group: the biggest, the most beautiful. A very common pattern is superlative + ever + present perfect: It's the best film I've ever seen. After superlatives use in with places: the tallest building in the city.
structure: the + -est / the most + adjective (+ I've ever + participle)
examples_en: It's the most honest city in the world, according to the test.
That was the worst meal I've ever eaten.
She's the friendliest person in our office.
This is the most interesting museum I've ever visited.
tip: 'The best film I've ever seen' — ever + present perfect after a superlative.

rule_en: too + adjective = more than is good (too tired); too much + uncountable, too many + countable. Enough goes AFTER adjectives (not warm enough) but BEFORE nouns (enough time, enough vegetables). not...enough = less than is needed.
structure: too + adj; too much/many + noun; adj + enough; enough + noun
examples_en: I eat too much sugar and I don't do enough exercise.
There are too many cars in the city centre.
This soup isn't hot enough.
Do you drink enough water?

rule_en: Use will/won't + base verb for predictions about the future, often with I think, probably, definitely: I think it'll rain. He probably won't come. Will is the same for all persons.
examples_en: I think our team will win tomorrow.
You'll love this book — it's brilliant.
She probably won't agree with us.
Life will be very different in fifty years.
tip: Position: 'probably' after will but before won't: 'will probably go' / 'probably won't go'.

rule_en: Use will for instant decisions (I'll take this one), promises (I'll always help you), offers (I'll carry that) and requests. Use Shall I...? / Shall we...? for offers and suggestions: Shall I open the window? Shall we start?
examples_en: It's cold — I'll close the window.
I'll pay you back on Friday, I promise.
Shall I help you with those bags?
Shall we take a break?
tip: 'Shall' is used mainly with I and we in offers and suggestions.

topic: review of verb forms: present, past and future
rule_en: Choose the tense by meaning: present simple (habits), present continuous (now/arrangements), past simple (finished past), past continuous (in progress in the past), going to (plans/evidence), will (predictions/decisions). Signal words help: usually, now, yesterday, while, tomorrow, next week.
structure: tense according to time and meaning
examples_en: I usually dream in colour, but last night I dreamt in black and white.
She's sleeping now — call back later.
While I was dreaming, my alarm rang.
Scientists think we'll understand dreams better soon.
tip: Find the time word first, then choose the tense.
